title: Introduction to Sanskrit
content: Sanskrit (संस्कृतम्) is one of the oldest languages in the world. The word 'Sanskrit' means 'refined' or 'perfected'. It is the classical language of India and the liturgical language of Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. Sanskrit has a highly systematic grammar, described by the ancient grammarian Pāṇini. It uses the Devanagari script, which is also used by Hindi and other Indian languages. Sanskrit is known for its precision and its rich literary tradition spanning thousands of years.

practice.question: What does the word 'Sanskrit' (संस्कृतम्) literally mean?

title: Basic Vocabulary
content: Let us learn some common Sanskrit words. Sanskrit vocabulary covers everyday objects, nature, people, and abstract concepts. Each word has a grammatical gender (masculine, feminine, or neuter) and a root form. Learning these basic words will help you understand simple sentences.

practice.question: What is the Sanskrit word for 'water'?

title: Pronouns
content: Pronouns replace nouns in a sentence. Sanskrit pronouns change form based on person (first, second, third), number (singular, dual, plural), and gender (for third person). Let us start with the singular forms.

practice.question: How do you say 'I' in Sanskrit?

title: Nouns and Gender
content: Every Sanskrit noun has a grammatical gender that affects how it changes form. Masculine nouns often end in -अः in the nominative case (रामः, बालकः). Feminine nouns often end in -आ or -ई (सीता, नदी). Neuter nouns often end in -अम् (फलम्, जलम्). Knowing the gender helps you use the correct adjective and pronoun forms.

practice.question: Which gender ending is -अम् typically associated with?

title: The Eight Cases
content: Sanskrit uses eight cases (विभक्ति) to show the role of a noun in a sentence. Unlike English, which uses word order and prepositions, Sanskrit changes the ending of the noun. The eight cases are: 1. Nominative (कर्ता — subject), 2. Accusative (कर्म — object), 3. Instrumental (करण — by/with), 4. Dative (सम्प्रदान — for/to), 5. Ablative (अपादान — from), 6. Genitive (सम्बन्ध — of), 7. Locative (अधिकरण — in/on/at), 8. Vocative (सम्बोधन — addressing).

practice.question: Which case marks the subject of a sentence?

title: Basic Verbs
content: Sanskrit verbs change form based on person and number. In present tense (लट् लकार), the basic pattern for third, second, and first person singular is: -ति, -सि, -मि. For example, from the root गम् (to go): गच्छति (he/she goes), गच्छसि (you go), गच्छामि (I go).

practice.question: What verb ending marks 'I' (first person singular) in present tense?

title: Simple Sentences
content: Sanskrit sentences typically follow Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) order. The subject is in the nominative case, the object is in the accusative case, and the verb comes last. Because case endings show the grammatical role, word order is flexible, but SOV is the standard.

practice.question: What is the standard word order in Sanskrit?

title: Introduction to Sandhi
content: Sandhi (सन्धि) means 'joining'. When Sanskrit words are spoken together, the sounds at their boundaries can change. For example, देव + आलयः = देवालयः (temple). This happens because अ + आ merges into आ. Sandhi makes Sanskrit flow naturally when spoken. There are three main types: vowel sandhi (स्वर सन्धि), consonant sandhi (व्यञ्जन सन्धि), and visarga sandhi (विसर्ग सन्धि).
